[56] aligned the gradient of LoRA with that of full fine-tuning by solving a minimization problem for this gap 2 2 2 We further discuss the relationship between this method and our method in Appendix E . . To fully exploit low-dimensional subspaces spanned by the columns of B B and A A , Zhu et al. [69] regularized those subspaces to capture complementary information. Along this, Li et al. [26] and Park et al. [41] exploited the geometry of Stiefel manifold that imposes the orthogonal constraints on B B and/or A A . On the other hand, exploiting the invariance of LoRA has been studied [ 63 , 50 ] . As explained in Sec. 1 , this approach induces preconditioning at each gradient step described in 4 and achieves efficient optimization compared to the original LoRA. This approach is the first Riemannian preconditioning study for LoRA, and its underlying idea is inspired by the classical low-rank matrix completion problem [ 36 ] . Note that, in the literature on low-rank matrix (or tensor) completion problem, several preconditioning variants have been proposed [ 51 , 65 , 64 ] . Our work follows the Riemannian preconditioning for LoRA proposed in [ 63 , 50 ] but designs a Riemannian metric tailored to LoRA for more efficient optimization.

Others. To improve the performance of LoRA, several LoRA variants have been proposed. Hayou et al. [19] applied different learning rates to B B and A A and shows fast convergence. Liu et al. [29] decomposed the pre-trained weight into magnitude and direction, and then employed LoRA for directional updates to reduce the number of trainable parameters. Xia et al. [59] trained multiple LoRA sequentially like the residual learning to improve the performance of LoRA. Dettmers et al. [11] applied quantization to the pre-trained models with LoRA to save memory usage without sacrificing performance. We leave the combination of these studies with our method to future work.

Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. The Muon optimizer for deep learning works by orthogonalizing the update matrix ( Jordan et al., 2024b ) . Unlike many other proposed optimizers, this has been highly successful empirically for training large language models, especially when coupled with weight decay ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . This is because the matrix can be orthogonalized relatively efficiently, using methods such as Newton-Schulz or Polar Express ( Amsel et al., 2026 ) . The orthogonalization step can be thought of as applying the matrix sign function to the gradient matrix, which normalizes all the singular values to one, prompting the question of whether Muon’s success comes from amplifying small but important directions with small singular values ignored by standard gradient descent, or from normalizing large, degenerate directions with large singular values that misdirect the training. In this paper, we will explore a method to target this orthogonalization to singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ \tau , and we will also experiment with different values for this threshold, thus allowing us to interpolate between SGD and Muon with a spectrally targeted version. Specifically, we will apply these Muon variants to the two speedrun tasks originally used to show Muon’s performance, the CIFAR-10 dataset with a convolutional network, and the NanoGPT large language model, just as in Jordan et al. (2024b) . In addition to standard performance metrics, we will examine other metrics more pertinent to the linear-algebraic structure of our weight and update matrices. This allows us to explore what characteristics of matrix optimizers lead to richer learning.

Recent Muon variants like NorMuon and Aurora mitigate neural death in Muon via sophisticated row-wise (neuron) normalization ( Li et al., 2025 ; Dewulf et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, our approach normalizes singular values to explicitly target the weights’ underlying linear structure. passages.text: Tool-using agents repeatedly carry observations whose useful content can be much smaller than their original payload. We study agent-controlled forgetting: the acting model selects previously observed tool results, replaces each with a short note at its original position, and retains the exact original in a recoverable archive. A Python harness exposes batch archival and explicit recovery without task-specific model training, while protecting user instructions and assistant messages from these operations. In an exploratory OpenTelemetry debugging case followed by an unrelated implementation task, the method ended with 231,951 provider-reported prompt tokens versus 912,492 under retained history, used 50% fewer cumulative input tokens, and had an estimated API cost of $1.28–$1.44 versus approximately $4.38. Both arms passed the two-case primary behavioral oracle; neither fully satisfied the follow-up evaluation. The method made more requests and took 17% longer. A contrasting application-development pair produced no context or cost saving, and an earlier continuation exhibited lower manually assessed quality despite reduced context. These observations demonstrate substantial resource savings in noisy tool-use trajectories and identify workload dependence as a central consideration for reversible context management.

The environment uses the public OpenTelemetry Demo source before an upstream checkout fix, at commit af3dc6553d9f7aebb5929b192fbf3a922a467050 . The primary task is to diagnose a failing checkout using browser and observability surfaces, implement a safe frontend error contract, and verify it. Background load and concurrent payment, advertising, image, Kafka, homepage, and product-catalog faults produce realistic competing observations. No prose padding or mandatory reading volume is injected. The fraction of irrelevant material is not independently annotated. After primary submission, the same session receives an unrelated C++ currency-service task requiring graceful shutdown. Each condition carries its own actual primary history and workspace into this phase. Consequently, the follow-up compares full trajectories, not an identical-history intervention that isolates the effect of the pivot itself. Retained runs first and method second. Each starts from a reset stack and a byte-identical source snapshot. Shared model configuration, task contracts, application setup, and task tools are held fixed; curation instructions and tools differ by design. Live telemetry, browsing choices, and generated code are not identical across conditions. The runner configures 1,500 logical calls and 1,800 provider attempts per episode, with a 131,072-token output budget and requested low reasoning effort. Neither condition reaches those limits. No fixed provider sampling seed or explicit temperature is supplied in this runner. The private primary oracle rebuilds a copy of the candidate and runs two upstream-derived Cypress cases. Both baseline failure and gold success were checked. Passing those cases supports the tested error behavior, not exhaustive satisfaction of every prose requirement.

The currency grader combines compilation, process probes, and source-text checks. It tests SIGTERM and SIGINT, process identity, exit status, elapsed time, and an occupied-port startup failure. Its six-criterion summary additionally uses string and regular-expression checks for implementation structure and reporting. The baseline scores 0/6 and the reference 6/6. However, calibration on one reference cannot establish general grader validity: alternative correct implementations may fail static patterns, and matching a pattern does not prove semantics. We therefore emphasize executable observations and treat the aggregate follow-up score as provisional supporting evidence. Thirty-seven benchmark inputs and a 605-file snapshot were frozen before the final pair. Version 01 had a compromised follow-up build surface and an incompletely specified primary error contract. A retained-only version-02 development episode exposed further deadline-contract ambiguity. Those trajectories are retained but excluded from the version-03 comparison. No post-grading repairs or selective reruns were applied to its candidates.

Planroom. A multi-phase application-development task requires library-documentation research through Context7, implementation, and twelve prescribed browser journeys through Playwright. Both arms use the same specification and scaffold, with a completion gate binding criterion identifiers to their full requirement text. Journey coverage is assessed from traces and independent checks. Model-written test counts differ and are not comparable accuracy denominators. File-picker behavior and deliberate persistence-failure injection remain evaluation gaps. Sphinx publication manifest. Six fresh sessions receive three successive implementation requests on Sphinx 8.2.3. The predefined order is retained, method, method, retained, retained, method. Private graders contain 11, 20, and 24 cases across phases. This older experiment uses a 16,384-token output limit and a global 300-request guard. Its different configuration prevents treatment as a replication of the final OpenTelemetry interface. Cases within each grader share requirements and are not independent statistical samples.

Why retained history first, and context editing next. Retained history answers the initial deployment question: what changes when an acting agent gains explicit control over which tool results remain active? It measures the combined interface and prompting policy against keeping all observations. The next direct comparison should test this policy against threshold-triggered removal of older tool results, as documented in Anthropic’s context-editing documentation ( [ ref-anthropic_context_editing ] ). That comparison would ask whether task-aware selection, per-result notes, and recovery improve the resource–quality trade-off beyond automatic clearing. A controlled test should use the same acting model, tools, tasks, and output budget across conditions; a harness implementation of an analogous clearing policy must be distinguished from a test of the provider’s actual feature. This baseline is a priority for the next study and has not been evaluated in the present experiments. Cache and control. The cost result is compatible with reduced input outweighing cache disruption, but it does not identify the provider’s cache mechanics. More model decisions can coexist with lower total cost, as in OpenTelemetry, or with a small cost increase, as in Planroom. Curation frequency is consequently not a useful success metric on its own. ACON includes acting-agent and compressor calls in its practical API cost estimate but explicitly excludes input caching ( [ ref-kang_2025_acon ] ). Our accounting includes reported cache usage; the different workloads and models preclude a direct numerical comparison.

Agent-controlled forgetting provides an explicit way for a tool-using model to distinguish information it needed to inspect from information it still needs to carry. In the central noisy debugging case, reversible curation accompanies a 75% smaller final measured prompt, 50% less cumulative input, and substantially lower estimated API cost, while both arms pass the same two primary behavioral cases. The method also requires more actions and time, and follow-up correctness remains incomplete. Contrasting application development and an adverse continuation show that neither resource savings nor quality preservation follows automatically from a smaller active history. The practical result is that an agent can complete noisy tool-driven work with substantially less active context and repeated input, using explicit archival decisions during the task. The contrasting outcomes define where further comparisons and replication are needed.

LoRA adapts a pretrained weight matrix through a low-rank update B ​ A BA , where A A maps the layer input into a small intermediate representation and B B maps that representation to the output ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Fixing one factor reduces the number of trainable parameters, but also fixes either the input or output subspace available to the update. A spectral construction makes another choice: which singular directions of the pretrained weight should define that subspace? Cross-method comparisons can entangle these choices. MiCA fixes the output factor on bottom singular directions ( Rüdiger and Raschka, 2026 ) ; PiCa’s implementation fixes an input-side projector on top directions and shares the trainable output factor across layers ( Hwang et al., 2026 ) . These correspond to freezing B B and A A , respectively (Appendix C.3 ). Comparing them changes orientation, band and sharing at once. Their within-method band ablations, by contrast, hold orientation fixed. The asymmetry between LoRA factors is already known. Zhu et al. (2024) show that training B B while fixing A A is often more effective than the reverse, including experiments with spectral factors. LoRA-FA fixes A A for memory efficiency ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and LoRA+ improves training by assigning a larger learning rate to B B ( Hayou et al., 2024a ) . The question we address is narrower: how large is the frozen-factor contrast relative to the top-versus-bottom spectral contrast, and how does that comparison change with rank?

passages.text: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. We introduce SciCurateBench, a benchmark of 200 expert-annotated papers from major life-science journals that challenges systems to verify conjunctive biological experimental criteria from raw, unprocessed scientific literature. We show that plain LLMs and popular reasoning, tool-using, and feedback-based agents all struggle with this task. To study what makes the task tractable, we further propose LangPoli, an integrative system in which a policy agent generates natural language action guidelines that actor agents convert into executable tools. LangPoli showed strong performance on both Paper Classification (83.16% F1 vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and Structured Information Retrieval, and also improves re-ranking on the public benchmarks of LitSearch, BEIR, and TREC. We further explore curriculum transfer, a method that distills generalizable strategies from solved tasks to accelerate the solving of related problems. We hope this work facilitates research in truly practical scientific AI assistance. The anonymized pre-release can be found from https://anonymous.4open.science/r/scicuratebench-D885/ .

We show that popular LLM reasoning methods achieve only suboptimal performance on the benchmark. To further push performance and study the factors contributing to success, we propose LangPoli, a multi-agent framework that adaptively creates tools to retrieve information from heterogeneous documents and verify precise conditions in the query. Unlike code-action agents that couple planning and implementation in a single generation step, LangPoli separates a natural-language policy from environment-specific code synthesis. This enables the creation of dynamic tools tailored to each document’s unique structure. Actor agents then convert these verbal action guidelines into executable code to collect observations. A critic agent evaluates the accumulated evidence against the query predicates and provides info-gap feedback to the policy agent, creating a closed loop that enables self-improvement over iterations. We note that concepts such as the plan/action structure Wan et al. (2024) ; Erdogan et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) , code as action instead of predefined sets Wang et al. (2024b) ; Yuan et al. (2024) ; Wölflein et al. (2025) ; Nguyen et al. (2025) , evaluation using LLM agents Shinn et al. (2023) ; Miao et al. (2024) ; Zhuge et al. (2025) ; Yuan and Xie (2025) , and adaptive tool usage Schick et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Wang et al. (2025a) ; Chen et al. (2025) have been established in the field, and LangPoli is a domain-specific adaptation of these components for the underexplored task of scientific data curation. Still, benchmarking LangPoli and other methods on SciCurateBench reveals the difficulty of the task and provides insights into the factors contributing to success.

Figure 1: SciCurateBench promotes adaptive tool creation for efficiently exploring, analyzing, and summarizing heterogeneous scientific files, including manuscripts, supplementary data, and raw datasets. We provide comprehensive benchmarking of popular agentic AI baselines on scientific data curation, including plain LLMs, reasoning agents, tool-using agents, tool-creating agents, and feedback-based agents. Our experiments show that LangPoli is the only method that performs consistently well on both tasks of SciCurateBench, reaching 83.16% F1 on paper classification (vs. 58.22% for its base LLM) and 69.43% F1 on structured information retrieval (vs. 59.13% for the strongest baseline). The framework also shows strong performance on public benchmarks of LitSearch Ajith et al. (2024) , BEIR Thakur et al. (2021) , and TREC Craswell et al. (2020) , particularly excelling on long documents where its created tools enable efficient targeted exploration. We show that the tools generated by LangPoli maintain high execution success rates and code maintainability scores while effectively supporting the exploration process. Finally, we explore curriculum transfer, a form of knowledge distillation where successful tool creation sequences are refactored and transferred as structured curricula to accelerate performance on related tasks. This approach enables the system to leverage problem-solving strategies learned from previous curation tasks, further improving efficiency and effectiveness on new scientific data curation problems.

Several limitations should be noted. First, SciCurateBench currently contains 200 papers. Although its total content volume substantially exceeds that of many existing benchmarks, scale expansion is an important direction for future work. Second, the current benchmark focuses on life science research, and extending it to additional scientific domains remains an important direction. Third, LangPoli depends on capable base models, since it must generate goal-oriented, error-free code. The scope of our work is to address the important yet underexplored task of scientific data curation with a new benchmark dataset and to provide baseline methods. Although each component of LangPoli is based on established agentic AI works, we believe its integrative design yields meaningful insights into the problem. Future work may evaluate more recent methods in agentic programming and RAG.

The re-ranking task asks the system to re-rank the top candidates, retrieved by the base method such as BM25, to determine the final permutation. We observe that LangPoli outperforms the strong RankGPT baseline (Table 4 ). Improvements are clearer when the underlying retrieval method is simpler (e.g., BM25 compared to GritLM), suggesting that LangPoli effectively compensates for weaker initial retrieval while still providing gains on top of neural retrievers. Table 7 shows LangPoli improves performance compared to the baseline BM25 and RankGPT across query sources and paper venues. Table 8 reports re-ranking performance on three BEIR subsets (Touche, News, and Robust04) that have the longest document contexts in the dataset (640.24, 1123.73, and 806.84 average words, respectively). Across a diverse set of base LLMs, LangPoli consistently matches or outperforms RankGPT on most dataset–model combinations. Table 9 shows that LangPoli with GPT-4o-mini consistently outperforms RankGPT using the same base model. Overall, these results show that LangPoli generalizes beyond life science domain. More importantly, building on established agentic components, our integrative design benefits literature curation and information retrieval tasks. We introduce BulkBoost , a two-band spectral reweighting framework with fixed-rank and noise-calibrated variants. The latter uses split-minibatch gradient differences to calibrate a Marchenko–Pastur reference edge for Muon ’s Nesterov input, separating the bulk below the edge from the spikes above it. Both variants increase the bulk’s relative weight through one shared gain while preserving the Frobenius norm of each matrix’s unreweighted direction. For a fixed partition, our theory gives the first-order condition under which moving weight toward the bulk lowers the loss. It also quantifies the fraction of the maximal first-order improvement rate, over all per-mode reallocations, that two bands can capture. A polar-plus-low-rank representation enables an approximation without a full SVD, tracking only the spike subspace. Across 30 30 continued-pretraining settings spanning Pythia- 14 14 M to 410 410 M and six corpora, two-band reweighting is competitive with the fine-grained power-law profile of Freon ( Shumaylov et al., 2026 ) and outperforms Spectra ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . Measured against Muon ’s flat profile, Freon reduces final loss by 0.022 % 0.022\% of the pre-adaptation loss on average, whereas the two-band variants achieve reductions of 0.073 0.073 – 0.147 % 0.147\% . These observations suggest that useful departures from the flat profile are surprisingly low-dimensional: a single bulk-to-spike gain captures at least as much benefit as the fine-grained spectral profiles.

This bulk is weak direction by direction, yet it carries useful signal in aggregate. Giving it more relative weight lowers the loss after a single update in most tested states (Appendices D and E.2 ). 4. Competitive gains without fine-grained shaping. BB-Adaptive instead sets the split online from the noise edge. It needs no fraction search, but it costs more per step. The noise edge comes from a white Gaussian noise reference model, so it separates signal from noise only approximately. Our evaluation is restricted to Pythia continued pretraining under the reported tuning protocol. Extending the evaluation to other architectures and training regimes remains future work.

Pythia provides a public model suite designed for analysis across training and scale ( Biderman et al., 2023 ) . We use this setting to compare fixed-rank and noise-calibrated spectral reweighting from common pretrained checkpoints, under matched training-token budgets and a common validation protocol. This complements the from-scratch language-model training settings used by several related optimizers and evaluates both allocation and partition-selection rules during adaptation. Our comparisons distinguish validation loss and token efficiency from per-step computation and fraction-selection effort (Section 5 ).
